utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I apologise for the delay. In light of the delay, we may be sitting to 3.00, if it is okay with the parties and the Registry. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Speaker.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, to whom were the government, and, before the government, the ministerial council, answerable to in our system? De jure and de facto?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government, and, before that the ministerial council, were answerable to the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbian Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then the assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will tell you what the paragraph 52 [as interpreted] says of the pre-trial brief: "The government, and, before that, the ministerial council, was subordinated to Krajisnik and Karadzic and it was another mechanism for the implementation of their idea, their concept of ethnic division." What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that it's inaccurate and I can't imagine on what basis that conclusion could have been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Paragraph 52 of pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ninety-two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Speaking about the assembly, Mr. President, how were decisions made? What was the decision-making process? How did it unfold? Was it easy? Was it difficult? And how did it come about that very frequently decisions were unanimous?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision-making procedure in the assembly is the usual procedure common to other parliaments as well. Background material would be prepared for every agenda and that background material was usually distributed to MPs, but it was also not uncommon for that material to be distributed just before the session. Before the MPs would arrive, the material would be distributed, but sometimes that would be done during the session itself. In some cases, it was impossible to prepare the material in advance because of the wartime situation, so the MPs would see it at the session. There would be a debate, and all the MPs were able to express their will, put forward proposals, and suggest amendments to the proposed material. You will see in the documents, and all sorts of material that has been presented here as evidence, that the MPs were very independent in their thinking and influenced decision-making. As a rule, deputies' clubs would hold their sessions and these deputies' clubs would consist of MPs from all parties, independent parties, and the Serbian Renewal Movement. Very lively debates would be held at these sessions before they arrived at an understanding. Excuse me. Very often, proposals were considerably changed after debate, but because of the tensions and the wartime constraints, I, as the speaker, as well as the others, still did not spare any time, did not spare any effort to make these debates as complete as possible. The transcripts reflect some of that atmosphere and the conclusions may be completely different. My task in the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and later I tried my best to do the same in the assembly of Republika Srpska, I made sure that every participant in the debate, MPs, members of the government, and members of the Presidency, are able to participate actively, to give their contribution, and I tried to make sure that there would be no outvoting, because that's what had happened in the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina where we had been brutally outvoted and pushed aside. So I wanted to avoid that, and I tried to make sure that we reached the best possible solution through debate. I never put any constraints on the MPs but I tried to make sure that we avoid any kind of extremist debate that would lead to unlawful conclusions or decisions, or simply negative decisions. What was most important to me was that all the conclusions and decisions serve the cause of implementing our policy, but also never to violate the constitution, the laws, and not to make any decisions that could be detrimental. Our MPs, who were the most important players in this debate, had a dominant impact on the decisions, and those who initially put forward very extreme, radical proposals were eventually moderated by the majority. And in the overwhelming majority of cases, our views were eventually harmonised.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 7 and 8, one statement made by Mr. Krajisnik is missing, and that is that the assembly was trying to find solutions rather than simply make decisions by the majority outvoting the minority. I can ask Mr. Krajisnik to confirm whether he said that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's correct. Our policy was, and I pursued it in parliament, to arrive at harmonised solutions rather than make decisions in which there would be just a majority vote. We simply wanted to arrive at solutions, and that's what made our parliament cohesive and stable throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which parties had influence on the work of the assembly? What kind of influence and how much?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the deputies were members of the Serbian Democratic Party but there were also MPs from the Serbian Renewal Movement; MPs from the former Reformist Party, which was known as Markovic's party; then MPs who carried the legacy of the former Communist Party in the former communist regime, socialists from the previous system. And I believe, and I believe it can be confirmed by every MP, that all MPs were equal in their influence on decision-making, and I could never accept that the majority should impose their will on the rest, if MPs from the other parties had a different opinion. So treatment was equal. Everybody was able to influence decisions equally, and it was proposals that won the day, not the majority in the parliament. It was not just how many MPs were for, how many were against. Decisions were made by majority vote, but they were always preceded by meticulous work, making sure that nobody would feel offended or unjustly treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did that meticulous work on every proposal imply?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You used the catch phrase by which you are remembered by the MPs and other members of the leadership; namely, you used to say that wracking your brain is not the purpose of decision-making; in fact, it could be brainstorming. Brainstorming was needed for making proper decisions, a good, productive debate in the parliament. Sometimes we debated things so much that we forgot who originally made the proposal. And if we made a good decision, arrived at a good solution, it was thanks to the work and the contribution of everybody in the parliament. A solution was good if everybody in the end eventually accepted it as if they -- as if it was their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How long were our assembly sessions usually?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes they were endless. In other words, we took as long as it was necessary to arrive at a good solution. They lasted very long because I was not the only one who wanted to arrive at a good solution. It was the overwhelming majority of MPs who didn't want us to veer in the wrong direction. And if we almost arrived at a decision, debate would often restart, MPs would express their views, and efforts were made to avoid taking the wrong course and making a decision that would boomerang on us. There were mediators who followed and monitored every decision we made, and screened it rigorously. That our assembly sessions were very long, we can also see from the transcripts. There were some shorter sessions also, where we went through many points on the agenda very quickly, but those were routine items. Sometimes materials would be prepared in advance and decisions were to be made on these points as a formality. But there were other issues, matters of war and peace, the fate of our people, and that took long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 5, line 12, you said that sometimes one would forget originally who made the proposal. What did you mean? How come that when the solution was near, people would originally -- forget who originally had made the proposal?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to explain. If a proposal is put on the table, some sort of resolution, for instance, or a plan, or something like that that is important, proposals were made how to deal with it. Somebody would, for instance, propose how to phrase it, what solution to choose, how to shape it, and that would be followed by a long discussion. And that discussion would arrive at a good solution, although that was not originally the solution proposed. It was better than what the initial proponent suggested. And everybody would accept it and would accept -- and would accept it as if they had made it themselves. That's what I meant. Very often we would forget who intervened so wisely because everybody accepted that proposal as their own and would end up feeling that they contributed so much that it was almost as if they had made the proposal themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll read to you what's written in paragraph 81 of the pre-trial brief: "The assembly was essentially a party organ, discharging its legislative function in keeping with the policy charted by the Serbian Democratic Party, whose main vehicles were Karadzic and Krajisnik. You can see that from numerous decisions, conclusions and laws that were adopted unanimously and without deliberation." What would you say about this qualification of our National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would feel proud if it were correct, as far as I'm concerned, because that would mean that all proposals made were lawful and no decision was targeting a particular ethnic community or a segment of the people. However, that was not the case. The leadership had to intervene, to tone down extremist discussions. Sometimes people feel the need to say things that are not always politically correct or wise or even productive, but the entire composition of the parliament, as I have said a few minutes ago, that is to say all MPs from all parties, enjoyed equal treatment and the Serbian Democratic Party did not dominate as it was represented in this citation. What perhaps needs to be explained is this: With a victory of the nation-based parties, these nation-based parties were three movements, that was political homogenisation. One party united practically all the Muslims, another party consisted only of Croats, or nearly, and the third party comprised all Serbs. They were not national parties, but they represented the state policy of all the ethnic parties. And the Serbian Democratic Party represented the top, and I can confirm that the policy carried out by the Serbian Democratic Party was the policy that represented all the Serbian people. You could see that from talking to every individual in the street. All Serbs were not all members of that party but they all supported those policies. If it hadn't been the case, the assembly, the government, or the Presidency, would not have been able to pursue that policy. And it cannot be said that it was just the policy of one party. It's not true that it was the policy of the Serbian Democratic Party. It was the policy of all the MPs and the entire Serbian people throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To what degree was the assembly a centralised organ and to what extent could it exercise influence over municipalities, the organs of government, at grassroots level?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, during my testimony, I said that municipalities, especially in 1992 and onwards as well, were mini states because of the lack of communication, and so on. And after all, because of the financial situation, because the scant resources that were there were in the municipalities. They financed defence, their army. So the assembly of the Serb people, or rather the People's Assembly, was an environment where top policies were pursued, top-level policies, like those aimed at talks and so on. However, the assembly could not influence any of the authorities at municipal level. For example, I, as the speaker of the assembly, and the president of the Presidency as well, could not influence the president of any municipality. They were autonomous, they made decisions at their own level independently, and none of us had the right to influence those decisions. The government, according to the constitution, could influence municipalities, however to a very small degree. Municipalities, according to our constitution, were completely autonomous and basically separated from the central authorities, that is to say the assembly of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am going to tell you what paragraph 83 says of the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "The assembly was an important centralised forum for making policies and instructions public and disseminating them on the ground. At assembly sessions and at deputy club meetings, Karadzic gave instructions to MPs in terms of divisions at ethnic level;for example that no one could live with Muslims, that they would get instructions on the take-over of municipalities in government and municipalities and that the ultimate objective was to unite with Serbia," and so on and so forth. This assessment of the constitutional position and also the practical activities of the assembly; is that correct? And also this assessment of my powers and abilities to instruct MPs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judges, you can see exactly from all these documents, from all those stenographic notes, I do not remember a single instruction or decision that was obligatory for Municipal Assemblies. Perhaps there were some proclamation or whatever, but it was laws that the assembly passed. Like in any parliament, those laws were in force in the entire republic. However, politically speaking, as for this formulation that I heard just now, that the assembly said that somebody is supposed to commit crimes or pursue a policy of division, and so on, I assert that there are no such decisions in our stenographic notes. As for the second part of your question, whether the president, through the deputies' club and through the assembly gave instructions regarding ethnic separation, you can establish quite easily a principle of ethnic separation but not in a negative sense. In order to establish constituent units -- that is to say the principle of the Cutileiro Plan was that in territorial terms there be an internal ethnic delineation, that is to say where somebody has an absurd majority. However, these territories did not have to be cleansed; that is to say that there should be no other ethnicities living there. They were all supposed to be mixed. Of course, in every one of these constituent units, two of the peoples would be a minority and one would be an absolute majority because that is the basic principle of establishing constituent units. Now, this invocation of instructions and the rest, you can see how that was done at the assembly session on the 27th of March, 1992. And what kind of instructions came from the president, the then-president, Mr. Karadzic? He said quite clearly what his suggestions were to the MPs in terms of what they should be doing on the ground. And he said quite clearly -- I mean, there was a great deal of fear among the MPs. War was at our door-step. We all supported the JNA that was supposed to protect those who were attacked. We didn't want to attack anyone. We just want didn't to experience what had been experienced during the Second World War. So then there was this fear among the Members of Parliament, and President Karadzic said quite clearly then, war suits no one. Us, in particular. We support peace. The peace conference should advance. We should protect our own territories. We don't want to take anybody else's territory. Who remains in our unit should be an equal and equitable citizen, and we should not carry out any kind of discrimination. All of that is contained in these minutes. And this was just before the war started. This best -- this shows actually what kind of instructions this man is giving. It is not that he's calling for any kind of unlawful action. He is supporting peace and expressing his faith that there would not be a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the assembly prescribe the way in which soldiers should take their oath and was this law amended at some point, and, if so, why? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these things remain in one's memory for a long time. The oath and the greeting that was there, there was a long discussion that took place at different meetings with the representatives of our army. How do I put this? They wanted to keep practices from the communist days. So what was accepted by way of a plebiscite, if you will, was to create scope for the members of other ethnic groups and I think that that oath was corrected later, I think, and this kind of scope was given; namely, that in the future, it's not only members of the Serb people who would be members of the Army of Republika Srpska. There would be members of other ethnicities, other peoples as well. This was derived from the following: We had information to the effect that some units, well, not a great many, but some units consisting of members of other ethnic communities were part of the Republika Srpska so we didn't want them to feel uncomfortable in any way, and therefore we thought that this oath should be changed so that members of another ethnic community could also accept that. Now, I can say what was of crucial importance. On TV, we saw what the other side was doing. They said that they had all the Bosnians, all the Herzegovinians from all three ethnic communities there and their greeting was a purely Islamic greeting, which was certainly not pleasant for, say, members of the Serb people. In order to not have that kind of oath, this was corrected and adjusted to a maximum degree, although it was a difficult time but we wanted to make it acceptable for members of other ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 17498.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this adopted by the Presidency on the basis of some special authority and was this verified by the assembly? Can you read out loud the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I solemnly swear on my life and honour to defend the sovereignty, territory, independence and constitutional order of my fatherland, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to faithfully serve the interests of its peoples [Realtime transcript read in error "people"]. So help me God."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Instead of me it was Professor Plavsic who signed it, but did the assembly confirm all this as our decision? Did it have to confirm it and did it confirm?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every decision had to be confirmed by the assembly. You see, the secretary of the assembly verified this, certified that this is an authentic copy of the original. You can also find it in the Official Gazette where it was published, because without that it wouldn't have been valid. I just have to draw your attention to something else. It's the date that's very important here, the 25th of June. This was just before the patron saint's day of Republika Srpska, St. Vitus Day. And I remember that we had a debate about what I mentioned to you a moment ago; namely, we agreed on that with our soldiers, that is to say the representatives of the military. We needed to provide this manoeuvring space so that this oath would be acceptable for the members of all ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript, it is not stated correctly but the translation is correct. It says "peoples." So it's not "people" in the sense of demos but it's people in the sense of peoples. So on page 12, could that be corrected in the transcript? In the document it could be seen clearly. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4004, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In several places in the indictment, it says, and that is the very basis of the indictment, it says that I, and my associates, wanted an ethnically pure Republika Srpska, or, that is to say, a Serb entity. Can you tell us what this meant during the war in our terminology, that something should be cleansed, cleansed in what sense?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to explain that, I will just have to go briefly to the time before that. When we talked to Mr. Cutileiro, the three parties, that is, it was stated then that there should be an absolute and relative majority; that is to say, in one constituent unit there should be a maximum number of members of one people and then in the second one of a second people and the third, the third people. And I remember this one conversation with Mr. Izetbegovic, saying, Please, there should be as few of you as possible in our area and as few of us as possible in your area. Now, what was meant by this? How do we put this? To have the best possible delineation so that as many members of a particular people as possible should be in that ethnic unit. So when one says for one area, say that it's Serb, Croat or Muslim, that is actually in that area, that is to say in this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the majority or the absolute majority is that particular ethnic community. In the talks that followed, we started using that in order to emphasise that this is purely Croat territory, this is purely Muslim territory, this is purely Serb territory. It never meant that in an area where the population is mixed, to a larger or smaller degree, it should be cleansed so that the members of only one people would stay on. I mean, the people belonging to that constituent unit, or, rather, the people to whom that constituent unit belonged. How do I put this? These pure territories, that is simply supposed to emphasise who this belongs to. Perhaps this is being pointed out because somebody wanted that part of the territory to belong to another constituent unit. I'll give you an example. Very often we said Grahovo, Glamoc, Drvar, these are purely Serb territories. And in Drvar, the population was 90 per cent Serb; and in Grahovac, say, 70; in Glamoc, 80 per cent, but that didn't mean that there weren't any others there. It just meant they were in an absolute majority. Perhaps it would be best to say that the word pure territories were territories where there was an absolute majority. Before the war, nobody advocated any kind of population relocation or that somebody should be forcibly expelled. Whatever happened during the war is a product of the war. And then some areas, where there was a particular percentage of one or the other or yet the other, there was a certain percentage of a particular people because there were these movements. But before the war, the policy was, and all the plans envisaged that, that the situation would remain the same and that nobody should be moved from anywhere. And these areas that belonged to particular units should belong to that unit, but there would be national minorities there too. So all the terms that were used were an aspect of our nature, where every nation or people emphasised something in order to protect it from the others who were trying to appropriate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in this process, while this was being established, were the territories divided into a contested and uncontested or disputed and undisputed territories, and how would you connect it with this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, you can see from an example, there is a map in Mr. Owen's book - that's the best way to understand it - where those disputed and undisputed territories are marked. What were these territories? In the beginning each national community provided its own map. The map showed the claims with regard to certain territories which the community claimed belonged to it, and then when we put those maps one on top of the other then we could establish which were the undisputed territories, those where members of one national community would accept that everything that is not on their map belongs to the other two national communities. In that way, and because of that, we had the disputed and undisputed territories. In terms of percentage, we agreed about perhaps 80 per cent as undisputed territories and perhaps 20 per cent or less were the disputed territories, where due to the ethnic composition and various reasons one national community claimed that it belonged to it and at the same time perhaps another one or two national communities also claimed that it should belong to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the allegations about ethnic cleansing, paragraph 105 of the pre-trial brief, it is claimed that the Crisis Staffs requested that the army should collect or take prisoner as many Muslims as possible and that in that way they directed the moving out of civilians, that they organised convoys in order to facilitate expulsion, they provided buses, police escort, they controlled detention facilities, provided support, and so on and so forth. Did the army carry out such tasks and respond to such requests? First of all, as a rule, did the Crisis Staff do this and express such requests vis-a-vis the army, and did the army do all of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To be precise, why don't we upload the pre-trial brief and see exact passage. Are they in e-court? I'm not sure. I have it before me but what paragraph -- where in paragraph 105, Crisis Staff ordering or requesting the army?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 105, unless there has been some change as I transferred it into word, it says: Immediately on establishing control in municipalities, and so on and so forth. And then the next bullet: They monitored in great numbers the removal of non-Serbs which was performed by Territorial Defence, police and the army. The Crisis Staffs requested from the army, and then there is footnote 241, to collect or take prisoners, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. In the main text it says: Crisis Staff implemented some measures. And in the first bullet point, referring to overseeing and requesting the army. Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the question, Mr. Speaker?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. The Crisis Staffs -- perhaps we should be more precise. My answer should be precise. Up until the moment when the army was established, and that was in mid-June, early on, when the war broke out, armed people were left in the field. There was no army. The people defended themselves in their own way. The Crisis Staffs already existed at that time during the first stage and up until the government's intervention to the effect that the Crisis Staffs should be disbanded and lawful authorities set up. The Crisis Staffs had no time to carry out this activity because they lasted for a short while. Nor was that part of their authority. Nor did the army exist at the time. I think that this conclusion, with all due respect for the OTP, is wrong because it was impossible to implement something like this because the army and the Crisis Staff did not exist simultaneously. This was also not within the purview of the Crisis Staffs, nor was the army supposed to obey them. The Crisis Staffs did not exist when the army did, and when there were some movements of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did we take over any responsibilities and obligations? And what were our obligations vis-a-vis the removal of civilian population from the areas where war was being waged?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are documents available, and I know specifically that the ICRC signed an agreement with the three sides to the effect that if in certain areas the situation would become difficult, and certain structures of the population would become vulnerable, it should be made possible for the population, if it so wished, to move from there with the idea that they would be able to return to their homes once the situation that was dangerous for some groups, especially those who were in the minority, would pass. And there are agreements, and on your behalf I think it was the then-MUP minister, Mr. Kalinic, who signed the document; on behalf of the Muslim side, I think it was Mr. Trnka or Mr. Kurjak; and also Mr. Coric as the representative of the Croatian side. So it was our obligation, according to this agreement, that if a certain group of the population expressed the wish and if they could be considered vulnerable part of the population, that it -- we would have to ensure to make it possible for them to leave. And under the auspices and with the agreement of international representatives, we took on ourselves the responsibilities that after the end of the war, such a situation - it could be perhaps during the war - that everyone would be entitled to return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it your mistake, by any chance, or was it the transcript, Mr. Kalinic, what was he a minister of?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kalinic was the minister of health and social protection, if I remember his title correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have in mind the first such agreement dated the 22nd of May and were there later consecutive agreements as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember all these activities quite well, as early as in the month of April. During the first visit of Mr. Cutileiro, it was announced to us that we would soon be signing such agreements. That was in Ilidza. After that, there was an agreement which I believe in Geneva was signed by Mr. Kalinic. This was followed by another agreement or two which were supplements to this one, as early as in September or perhaps even earlier, and there are documents available in this Tribunal, Mr. Samaruga and other high-ranking ICRC officials gave statements including the provisions and practically quoting excerpts from the agreement which we had accepted and which Mr. Kalinic had signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the witness 1D49012 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please focus on - we have the translation now as well - saving lives in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Geneva, 3 October 1992, a statement of Cornelius Samaruga, securing humanitarian aid and so on. The second bullet here says: Facilitate the transfer of the most vulnerable civilians and those wishing to be reunited with their families and allow them to reach safe areas. And the rest deals with prisoners and so on, and there is an appeal addressed to Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Boban, and me to facilitate this. What was our position with regard to all this? And excuse me, the second bullet says: Facilitate those wishing to be reunited with their families and allow them to reach safe areas, to join their families and resettle in safe areas or in other country until they can return to their homes. What was our position? Did we accept this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This provision precisely has to do with what I just said a little while ago. The basis of our obligation was to make it possible for all vulnerable categories of civilians and those who wished to leave certain areas because of the war to do so. And this is just a provision which is quoted here. Our position was that every man should be guaranteed freedom of movement with the condition that everyone was entitled to return to his or her home. No one could leave unless they expressed their wish to do so, nor did anyone have the right to expel anyone. If someone used force to expel somebody, it could mean an individual who certainly violated our policy and the provisions and the agreement through which we accepted this obligation, that is to say which we had accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is this document, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the statement of Cornelius Samaruga given in Geneva on the 3rd of October, 1992, on the occasion of our talks. I'm not sure from which part it originates, but I believe it has the ERN number so we can establish that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do you see an ERN number? But I will ask Mr. Tieger first. Do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes to the extent that it appears to be an excerpted -- it appears to be excerpts which are compiled for a particular purpose. So it doesn't -- as far as I can tell, it's not the statement. It's some portion of -- purports to be some portion of what was said that omits the entirety of the statement for this Court's review and our review. So that's a problem. I don't have a particular reason to think that there is an inaccuracy in the excerpted portion but it's quite something else to lift it out, compile it in another kind of document, and then present it to the Court as if it's the entirety of what was stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The B/C/S seems to be marked as an original. And I'm wondering why the page 3, page 4 markings, such as those, should appear. And I saw a note in English that the English was taken from the Red Cross original and divergences from the B/C/S version were marked, if I read -- if I were to read it that way. Exhibit from which case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know. We found it in IDS. Perhaps we could zoom out a little bit to see if there is an ERN number. To zoom out of the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification until we hear from the parties as to the provenance of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It also appears, based on what I see handwritten at the top of the Serbian version, to have been a document tendered by the Defence in another case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That was my question, yes. We will mark it for identification for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4005, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English version has a number on the bottom, it's an identification number, and I believe it's the ERN number, but never mind. Could we now please show 1D49011.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is from the same year but two months later, the 4th of December. Jean de Courten, director of operations. Can you please have a look at it? Do you remember this document, and can you just check it out for the substance?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, I think that the previous document and this one are from my case, and that these are D227. You can check but I think it was from the appeal because I'm quite familiar with both of these documents. I cannot assert that whether this was my number or not but both documents were used in my case and were admitted, as far as I remember. Namely, I can read here that in view of the gravity of the situation, the ICRC had had to deploy over 150 delegates in the former Yugoslavia, most of them are working in Bosnia-Herzegovina endeavouring to improve compliance with international humanitarian law by the parties to the conflict. Bring assistance to some 500.000 displaced persons and 40.000 needy people housed in hospitals and other institutions throughout the 80 per cent of the republic's territory now accessible to ICRC delegates, protect the civilian population, and so on. This tells you that it's, in fact, the implementation of the agreements which were signed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is how I interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Same issues presented, Mr. President, so I presume the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will mark it for identification as Exhibit D4006 until we hear the provenance of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the same document we read that convoys were organised and police escort was provided. The agreements you mentioned, the one signed by Minister Kalinic, was it these agreements that made it incumbent upon us to make sure that these convoys have police protection, police escort?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly the language of the agreement, but I remember that the population could move only in an organised way, voluntarily, after expressly declaring their will to leave. The purpose of these movements was not to change the ethnic composition, so it was not ethnic cleansing. Ethnic cleansing would have occurred if a certain minority was expelled in a different way.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic start over? And we don't have the text of the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You are asked to start over. Please bear in mind that the interpreters do not have the pre-trial brief with them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The paragraph is 72 of the pre-trial brief. It claims that Karadzic and Krajisnik maintained their top positions in decision-making and controlling the authorities in Republika Srpska, which they had had even before the establishment of the Presidency and the election of the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you, or did I, have a leading position, a top position, in controlling the authorities of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am concerned, it looks like somebody is being rewarded with a medal. I believe, with all due respect to the Prosecutor, that this paragraph is wrong. There was no individual or even a group that had such power. It was collective thinking and collective decision-making after long, profound discussions. I don't know exactly what people imagined. Our people have a tendency to crave leaders and make a fetish of their importance, but the way it is written here it is power that not even a king could have had in the past, let alone two people like you and I in a time when everybody who had a rifle and had freed up some territory had power. I believe that this is a figment of somebody's imagination, or maybe popular imagination. I was indeed in a public office. I was in a position of authority. And I was able to do a lot. But certainly not that much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you started your answer by saying, as far as I'm concerned, and ended with -- that you were indeed a public office -- in a public office. What would you say with respect to Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was trying to tell you what I feel and what is the most authentic concerning my role because I am closely tied here with Mr. Karadzic. And as I said at the end of my answer, even our kings in the past did not have such power as is ascribed to me and Mr. Karadzic. This is practically making a fetish of a leader. Our people like to ascribe to their leaders a power that royalty had in the past. And whatever I said in my answer applies to Mr. Karadzic as well. Briefly, this paragraph is wrong. Mr. Karadzic did not have such power, if we are talking about him now, and I believe this is a wrong idea in the heads of some people. In reality, it was far from the actual powers that Mr. Karadzic or I had.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 24, line 23, I don't think the interpretation is quite right. The witness said: As far as I'm concerned, it would have been as if somebody had rewarded me with a medal, if I had had such powers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could just confirm whether that was correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I didn't put it very well, but I said this description of my importance looks like a nomination, like somebody nominating me for an award. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I'll be brief. I'll finish soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, you spoke a little about Mr. Holbrooke, that some things were put down in writing, others were not. Which part was never written down? Which part remained a verbal agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was not written down was the undertaking by Mr. Holbrooke; namely, that The Hague Tribunal and its indictment would be history for Mr. Karadzic if he withdraws from public life. And what is written down is the part of the agreement that you should withdraw from all official positions and public life.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness 1D05920. And before we put it up, I'd like to know if there are any restrictions on this document. There are none, I'm told. We only have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you know the name of this ambassador, Mr. Menzies, and did you meet on 22nd July, 1996? Look at paragraph 2, summary.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could just tell me from what country he was, it could help me remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The United States.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did meet with the US ambassador at the time. Soon after that he left and the secretary of the embassy later became ambassador. That's why I'm confusing the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you look at 3(C). "Ambassador DCM and Poloff met with RC assembly president, Momcilo Krajisnik, and GORS [In English] Minister Aleksa Buha in Pale July 22nd. Ambassador reported to Krajisnik and Buha that he had spoken with Holbrooke July 21st, and that Holbrooke had reported to Washington on the written and oral agreements reached with the GORS representatives in Belgrade." [Interpretation] In your view, what is this oral agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I did speak to the US ambassador, and if I'm allowed to interpret this text, I know that this oral agreement is exactly what I described earlier. The oral agreement, which is not in the written agreement, is that The Hague Tribunal would be history for Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Holbrooke confirmed that at the end, and the participants in that meeting can all confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you gain the impression while meeting with Ambassador Holbrooke that he believed that I was really responsible and culpable and guilty and would he have entered such agreements if I had -- if he really believed I had perpetrated such acts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just ask him the impression of Mr. Holbrooke. Or how could he know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the reason for their demands for me to withdraw from political life, and did they express any conviction that I was really the perpetrator of any wrong doing?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my impression: Mr. Holbrooke believed it was very important in the continued implementation of the peace accords, that Mr. Karadzic be removed from that implementation and he believed that the indictment does not serve that purpose. In other words, we'll withdraw the indictment as a threat, and you will withdraw and we'll continue to implement the Dayton Accords. That's how he thought the Dayton Accords would be implemented more easily. It's also true, however, that he let us know he didn't want to go into whether the indictment is based in fact or not. He was only looking at whether the indictment was serving the purpose of implementing the Dayton Accords or it could be in the way. My impression is that he didn't believe Mr. Karadzic was guilty. Otherwise, he wouldn't undertake to have the indictment withdrawn. He wouldn't undertake to do that if he had believed the indictment to be based in fact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, can we see the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I forgot this. I'll read it. Line 4: [In English] "Buha was in the role of good cop, as much as possible. In a private aside with the ambassador after the meeting, Buha explained the alleged Holbrooke proposal for The Hague Tribunal to vanish after September elections." [Interpretation] How does this fit into what you had and learned at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is precisely true because Mr. Buha asked Mr. Holbrooke at the end, So where are we finally? And he said, The Hague Tribunal will no longer be a concern to Mr. Karadzic. The only thing that matters is that he withdraw and abide by this agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted? I have no further questions for Mr. Krajisnik, and I thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is GORS the abbreviation of?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For example, can you take a look at page 1? In paragraph 2(C) we see some blank lines with two markings of confidential. Does it mean that that part has been redacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. This document has been provided to us in full. And if you see the end of the line before the word "confidential" and the first line of the text under the word "page 2," it continues to read in logical sequence. So I think it's just the way the document was printed. But this was fully, as it says in the top right, released in full to us. It was filed by us in connection with the Holbrooke agreement motion in 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Any objections, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4007, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We shall have a break, after which we'll hear the evidence of other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. Mr. Puhalic will be testifying next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik's cross-examination shall begin probably on Wednesday next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe on Tuesday of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tuesday. Do you understand that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Can I just say one sentence? I would like to thank you for having made it possible for me to get the documents from this trial which will assist my review. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.15 -- 16, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I told you that the Chamber would deal with the Kovac's interview after Mr. Krajisnik's in-chief testimony, but we'll deal with it first thing tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. There is a matter I'd like to discuss in closed session. Could we move into closed session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The witness is already in and would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I get up? I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Puhalic. Just bear with me a minute. Yes. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Puhalic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor or even from Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "Incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony, compelled under such circumstances, would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Puhalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Puhalic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you to pause between what I say and what you say. I also have to ask you that we both speak slower than we speak usually, and I'm a fast speaker myself. We need to do this in order to have everything recorded in the transcript. Did you give my Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D9280 in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see your statement on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the last page please be displayed so that the witness could identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This statement, does it faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to read this out to you today, or actually, if I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I would like to tender this statement on the basis of 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering any associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The video that was mentioned in the end of the statement is being tendered as an associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has it been uploaded on to e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's been uploaded and I believe that the CD was given to the Chamber and the parties earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would object to its admission at this stage. There is no foundation been laid as to where the excerpt is from and how it was created.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's deal with the 92 ter statement first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4008, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Instead of hearing from the parties, could you -- I wonder whether Mr. Karadzic could deal with this live, the video tape, with the witness. That may be the easiest way. And hear -- I will hear from Ms. Sutherland then. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. First of all, I would like to read a brief summary of Mr. Slavko Puhalic's statement in the English language and then we would deal with this video. [In English] Slavko Puhalic was a member of the Prijedor 343rd Motorised Brigade until April 1992. It was the JNA brigade. He was requested to join Major Slobodan Kuruzovic, warden of Trnopolje camp, in a role as a logistics soldier mainly involved in the procurement of food. Slavko Puhalic considers that the primary purpose of the Trnopolje camp was to accommodate non-Serbian civilians from the zone of combat operations, who were held for their personal safety and that of their family. The Red Cross guaranteed the civilians' arrival and they were then registered. The civilians were allowed to leave the camp freely. Some civilians would go abroad after they had been issued with the relevant documents from the Red Cross. The security in the camp was organised in the form of guard duty and the primary purpose of this was to prevent unauthorised persons from entering the camp. Slavko Puhalic was aware that Major Kuruzovic asked everyone at the camp to act in accordance with international humanitarian law. Major Kuruzovic warned his subordinates to discharge their duties in the best way possible, but he would not have known everything that went on in the camp. Slavko Puhalic considers that the capacity of the camp was limited and there was not enough room, there was a field kitchen that could prepare a limited number of meals. There was an infirmary at the camp if medical assistance was required. To Slavko Puhalic's knowledge, civilians primarily came seeking protection and safety and stayed until conditions were created for them to leave the territory. He himself helped a number of people gain safe passage to Prijedor. He did not hear officials of Prijedor order ethnic cleansing and there was no mention that Prijedor should be solely Serbian. Slavko Puhalic recalls one visit by foreign journalists who were allowed to film inside and outside the camp, and talk to anyone that they wanted to. No preparations were made for the journalists' arrival and the fencing that surrounded the camp was not altered from the original fencing that had been placed before the war. And that is a short summary. I would now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before putting questions about that video, I would like you to ask the witness what he meant by saying at the end of paragraph 8 that Major Kuruzovic could not have known everything. What did you mean by that major could not have known everything, and why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, he, as far as I noticed, was not there every day, and those who were there, who were the guards there, did not report to him or something like that about what happened every day, that is. Along those lines. So that's how he couldn't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like to ask for this video footage to be played, 1D4808.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you, Mr. Puhalic -- actually, I'm going to stop this from time to time so that I could put questions to you. Could you tell us what we see here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a building - how do I put this? - in Trnopolje. It's like a cultural centre, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what kind of fence this is? Who are these people we see here?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: These are the people who were there in the camp, who had arrived after the war operations that had started in Prijedor and the area around it. The people who came to that camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are these only civilians, or were there some people there who had taken part in the fighting there, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, these are civilians, and there were some friends of mine whom I knew from before, who were in the army of the BH, the group of the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now hear the sound track? Is this the visit of the journalist that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I'm not sure whether it's that or something else. I don't know. I'm not sure. I don't know. I don't know when this was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, would you like us to hear the sound?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There seems to be a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We'll try to go on working until this is overcome. 135, please, could we see that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Further, if you like us to hear the translation, probably you need to distribute the transcript to the interpreters in advance. I see they are nodding, that they have it. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you hear this? Who are these people here that are talking to the journalist? Oh, could you go back, please, these people who are talking to the journalist?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: These are the people who were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where are they in relation to this barbed wire?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Outside the barbed wire, on the external side of the wire. This is the wire, if I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please do. Explain what this schematic shows.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: The schematic shows this was a shop selling agricultural tools, and next to the shop there was also a warehouse, a storage area, where the goods were properly stored. The shop was fenced off with barbed wire, the fencing, so this camp, or how should I call it, the centre was not surrounded with barbed wire. There was a low metal fence, both around the cultural centre and around the school. But I don't know. I cannot exactly remember whether outside the school and in the direction of the houses was some other fence. And on the other side there was no fence, no wiring at all. It was a big field or a pitch, and there were no signs, no markings, no wire, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this schematic part of that video footage?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in order to explain this visually, and now I will ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue. We'll deal with the footage later on. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalic, we saw in the video that between the camera and the people who were recorded, there is some wire. What wire was that? And where were the people and where were the journalists?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: The people were outside of the wire and the journalists were inside.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you stop here, please and freeze.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see well here that the journalists are inside, that is the building or the facility, the shop, which was fenced off with the wire so the journalists are inside, on the inner side of the barbed wire fence and the men are outside of the fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is this vessel that can be seen here?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, Mr. Puhalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We call it a cart or a wheelbarrow, in order to use to transport some goods, such as firewood and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until we have the sound, can you tell us this: You mentioned that they had some health protection. What did that look like?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, look, I don't know whether it was so in the beginning, a doctor was there, perhaps one doctor or two, I cannot remember exactly. I know about one. There were also two or three nurses there. Later on, another doctor came from our side and also a medical orderly. He was there every day. They were present when this was organised. When the ICRC came, I mean, the army, and that -- when it was organised, that was when the doctor came, perhaps every -- perhaps even every day he came inside, he treated people, and tried to help them as much as he could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did these people feel, in terms of security, the people who were here at the camp, by comparison to other places outside of the camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Here, they -- as much as we and Major Kuruzovic managed to secure this, they felt much more free than elsewhere, in other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned the doctors, what were these doctors who were helping and providing assistance, by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: There were Muslim ones and Serb ones as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now try it with the sound, please. I think we got it. And it's with subtitles so I think we will be able to do it. Can we try it now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm told --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- in order to solve the technical difficulties, we need to rise for ten minutes. We will have a break for ten minutes. --- Break taken at 11.57 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would ask if we could now start playing from 16 seconds up until 40 seconds, 0016.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot find this in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall we stop. It's only two pages, and I see these on page 1. But interpreters said that they could not find the passage.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have a 15-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the -- there is a -- you have subtitles, you can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. But they say they have a 15-page document. What is it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Perhaps that's a different document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably it's a transcript of the entire video, we need from 0016 to 0045.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We don't have the time noted on the transcript, only numbers of lines from line 1 to line 51 on each consecutive page, so it's difficult to find any excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Note to the interpreters: They are coming. While it is being distributed, why don't we discuss about the provenance of this document. Is it an edited version on your side, Mr. Karadzic? Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, this is an excerpt of a longer film which is called "The judgement," which is broadcast on Serbian RTV so we have taken out portions that are relevant to this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this is an excerpt from the Serbian TV programme which used the image broadcast by Penny Marshall in other media?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the film can be watched on You Tube, the whole film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not a point. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand that there has also been information added to the ITN footage. As you could see the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, information was added by -- what was the name of the Serbian media?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's Serbian RTV, Radio TV Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, not by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. So it's the commentary and the diagram that we saw a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the reason for your objection to the admission, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness is only, thus far, been able to identify some of the buildings and structures at the camp. He cannot comment on the -- or hasn't commented and shouldn't comment on the commentary. That's of no value, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He confirmed the location of the barbed wire vis-a-vis the film crew and the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm saying that's as much as he's done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I had to come here. Those that did not fight came here. I came with children, small ones, here down the field. Nobody harassed us, nobody laid a finger on us. I stayed in the village up there."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How does this fit with what you know? Is this man telling the truth? How does this fit with what you know about the character of this camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: He's telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now if we can play from 050 to 059.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We have been here from the very first day. People came here on their own will, probably because of food shortages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was this woman's role and whether she is telling the truth, according to what you know? Is it correct what she is saying?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I can't remember, but that was probably a lady from the Red Cross. I cannot remember her name and I do believe that she's telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please start at 131?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Is it safe here? "I think it's very safe, but it's very hard." "Here's a little --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear the interpretation of what this man, Mehmed, or whatever his name is, was saying?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard two or three words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How does that fit with your experience and knowledge about this camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: He's telling the truth. It was safe but it was difficult. There was not much food, there were too many people, and they all needed to be fed. The conditions were poor there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you had an opportunity to learn how this camp was represented in the media after this visit took place? How was this depicted in the media? And did you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I didn't know much, really, but I heard from friends that it was a very unfavourable picture, what was reported, that it was a real prisoner camp, that people vented their anger, maltreated the inmates, and all kinds of things were said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at this picture now. You can see the one who spoke recently, Mehmed, and then a thin man. In your view, how did this happen? Did he get so thin while he was there at the camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly whether he lost weight in the camp or before his time there. I don't think that he could have acquired such a figure in such a short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I now tender the footage that we saw, those inserts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Now I'll hear from you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to the admission of this, if this -- the sound -- what I'm saying is the commentary by the people that have made this film is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the Defence agrees with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4009, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions at this stage, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Puhalic, as you have noted, except for the part related to this video footage, your evidence-in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is through your written statement. Now, you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland. Shall we continue till quarter to 1.00 when we break for lunch? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalic, the statement that you signed on Monday, the one that's just been admitted into evidence, when was the earlier draft taken?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: The first draft was, I think, at some point in January 2013, but I'm not exactly certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who took the statement from you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I gave the statement to the Defence. It was Mr., I believe, Todic was his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were the questions given, provided to you in advance or were they spoken to you as the statement was taken?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke with him, and as we had the conversation, he noted my answers and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm a bit perplexed as to when you got to the camp. In paragraph 3 of the statement, you say I quote, "After the camp was formed." And then further on in that same paragraph, you say, "In the beginning when the camp was formed." So what will it be, after the camp was formed or when the camp -- in the beginning, when the camp was formed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, now, whether it was a day or two or three, I cannot remember now. It was such a long time ago. Mr. Kuruzovic said that he was having some problems and that he couldn't manage, that he needed assistance, whether he got it from the army or -- we were both neighbours and friends, so he asked that somebody from the unit, namely myself, should come along with him up there and help him with those over there as there were many people who were arriving on trucks, tractors, personal cars, coming to the camp. He requested assistance from me, food was needed, and other things, and he wanted me to help about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've answered the question. You were getting on to food. That's why I stopped you. I would ask you to be as brief as you can in answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 5, of your statement, you're quite clear when you say you have no knowledge at whose orders the camp was formed because you were an ordinary soldier. That's right, isn't it? You have no knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
