utterances.text: You say that there were a couple of excesses in the beginning committed by people who broke into the camp, but that's not true, is it? There were murders of individuals in June and July, weren't there, by both camp personnel and soldiers coming to the camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So what about a large number of the Foric [phoen] family who were called out and killed? What about Ante Mrgic [phoen] and his son, Zoran, also killed in July? Tofik Talic [phoen] died as a result of beating in July. Sulejman Kekic [phoen] was killed by a guard in July. And soldiers came to the camp in July and took 11 men into a nearby maize field and killed them. Do you not know about these instances that happened in the camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, that -- I stated why I knew what happened, that is to say the information from people who were inside in the camp. I learned that and I wrote there what I do know. As for what I don't know, I can't tell you that because I was --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you were unaware of those -- those four instances of people being killed in the camp; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember all the people. For some I don't know what their names were. I said that I was aware of two or three instances where people lost their lives. And I noted in the beginning that there were several excesses, not to say beatings. Mr. Kuruzovic was informed about this. Whether he took some measures or not, he probably went to the police and requested from the army that these people be protected, but they were treated by the medical staff in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're saying in six months that the camp was in existence, you're aware of two or three people that lost their lives in that six months; is that right? It requires a yes or a no answer.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Rapes also occurred in the June and July. There was a woman who was systematically raped by the camp commander throughout July. There were several young women -- throughout August, I'm sorry. There were several young women taken out at night and raped or sexually assaulted in July. Now, you mentioned that there were -- you were aware of some rapes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And beating of individuals was a regular occurrence in the camp. Nedzad Jakupovic was badly beaten and treated in the clinic. He suffered an eye injury and injuries to his body, and he had wire marks cut into the skin of his arms which had been tied with wire during the beating. And another inmate who was beaten at the same time as he was killed as a result of his beating. Do you not recall this instance?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number P03896.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalic, that is photograph of Mr. Jakupovic. Do you recognise -- do you recall seeing injuries like that on -- on the detainees in Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No. I can't remember, and I was there at the camp until the 11th of June. After that, I went for a spa treatment that lasted up until around the 17th of July, and then I returned for another 10 or 15 days to Trnopolje, and then I was sent back to my unit, so I can't know everything. What I know, I have included in my statement, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just so I understand your evidence well, you were at the camp two or three days after it opened, at the end of May. You were there for approximately a fortnight until the 11th of June, and then you were there again from the 17th of July to around about the 27th of July. Is that what you're saying, those -- those were the only two periods you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly. Perhaps until the 15th of August. I can't remember the exact date when I returned to my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you didn't think it was relevant in any way to put in your statement that you were only in Trnopolje camp for 24 days out of six months?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Nobody asked me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. On your evidence that's been admitted, you're an ordinary soldier who has mainly procured food for the camp. We'll get to the food later, but for now let's talk about you. Of all the persons that were working at the Trnopolje camp in 1992, you're the only one, are you not, with the first name Slavko?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Maybe, there were more men called Slavko. I was not alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm talking about the people that were -- had the role of camp guards, camp security.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not a guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're the only Slavko who worked at Trnopolje who was a butcher by trade, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Maybe. I don't know who other people were by occupation, but it's true that I am Slavko and that I am a butcher by occupation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you remember Vasif Gutic, a medical student from Kozarac who was detained in Trnopolje and was in the infirmary?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I don't know who he is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He testified in the Tadic trial. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: A lot of time has passed since then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He testified in the Tadic trial in 1996 and he remembered you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who is he? We do not have --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Vasif Gutic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please put a pause. Please put a pause.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could have 65 ter number 25630.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At transcript page 4709, Mr. Gutic said that Slavko Puhalic had an office in the former office of the local commune building "where Slavko also took inmates for interrogation when they were interrogated, when he interrogated them and where some were beaten." You did take prisoners for interrogation, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No. There were some friends with whom I talked, just as I'm talking here. Maybe, I don't know. It wasn't an office. It was a little room, even downstairs where the dom itself was, where I was sitting, there was an Albanian gentleman, Izet Beri [phoen], I sat together with them, too, talking. Maybe something happened after me but there were no beatings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you participate in the beating of any person at Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What about being present during beatings?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I can't remember, really. It was a long time ago. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know a man called Adem Dzihic, also formerly from Kozarac who was detained in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He gave a statement to the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 25607.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There is a statement he gave in September 1994, and on page 3, he said: "The commander of the police, who guarded and interrogated the camp prisoners, was Slavko Puhalic, who used to own his butcher shop in Prijedor." That's you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I did not have a butcher shop. I worked as a butcher in a state-owned company.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You worked in a butcher shop in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document. Mladen Mitrovic and Goran Nisevic [phoen] were camp guards, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Probably. I can't remember the names of the guards anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 25 of your statement, you said in relation to adjudicated fact 1237 that in the beginning there were cases of mistreatment. You said there were a few cases that you knew of and reported these to Major Kuruzovic. Do you know Mustafa Nuhanovic, who was from Trnopolje and was detained in the camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, he knows you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I can't recall. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter number 25604, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say paragraph 25 of his statement, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's one of the new additional paragraphs. It's on page 9 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I probably only have the older version.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, Mustafa Nuhanovic testified also in the Tadic trial on the 7th of August, 1996, and at the bottom of page 4841, he was asked whether he was ever beaten in Trnopolje camp. And he said, Yes, several times. Were any times -- were there any times that were particularly severe? Twice, yes. Rather severe, he said. Where did they occur, he was asked. At the top of page 4842, he said, In the building next to the centre called laboratory. He was asked who took him there. He said Mladen Mitrovic. He was asked, When you were taken -- and this is at line 23 of that page, When you were taken to the lab and beaten, did you recognise any of people who took part in that beating? He answered, Yes. One Slavko from Prijedor, a captain by rank, I mean I saw the insignia, three stars, that is a captain, and he interrogated me. I do not know. He was a butcher in Prijedor. I believe his family name Pahovski or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to transcript page 4844, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He was asked during the first beating he received what was used to beat him with? And he said, at line 10, They beat me with anything from baseball bats to cables to boots, hands and even a chair. Did they appear to concentrate the blows on any parts of your body? Yes. Where, he was asked. He answered, In the area of my heart and kidneys but otherwise, all over the body. They beat all over, including my head. And the injuries he sustained, he said at line 19, The first time one of my veins in my leg is cut. My head is was fractured. It was broken here. There were fractures here like this, five or six centimetres, and I had many such injuries. On page 4845 he was asked about the second beating, Who was that, who took you for the second beating? Oh, it was the same man, so to speak, that Mladen, but there were others too who were in his company. Cigo was there. And he said that Cigo's last name was Nisevic, Goran Nisevic. And at page 4846, Did you lose consciousness during either time you were beaten. He said, Yes, they beat me and beat me. I do not even remember how long. It looked like eternity to me. Eventually one took me by my feet and put me against the wall and the other one began to beat me with his hands, with his feet, so that I felt sick. I threw up. Then suddenly I wanted to throw up again and I could not, and there was some yellow liquid which I vomited. It was so bitter that I have never tasted in my life anything so bitter and then I must have fainted. He was asked, Were you ever told why you were beaten? Yes, several times. Why were they beating you? They were asking for rifle, for money, for gold. Now, Mustafa Nuhanovic remembered that you participated in one of his beatings at the camp. Do you remember being involved in this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: First of all, I've told you I was a simple soldier, without any rank. Maybe there was another Slavko, a captain, that I can't remember. But I don't know this person, nor did I participate in these beatings. I can't remember this Mitrovic, or what did you say he was called, Cigo? I can't remember these people, I didn't participate in that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You had a level of authority in the camp to stop detainees being mistreated, if you wanted to, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I did not have any authority but I tried to help people as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In fact you took money from detainees on the proviso that you'd stop bad things happening like being beaten by guards, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You know a person by the name of Rifet Zenkic? He's around 14 years older than you. You were a neighbour of his sister's daughter? You took money from him in payment for stopping Skrbic from beating his son, didn't you? Why are you smirking, Mr. Puhalic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I really cannot remember. I'm really sorry but such things I just can't understand it. He's lying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 25606, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a statement taken from Mr. Zenkic in August/September 1994 so a couple of years after the event. Page 11 of the statement, he's talking about his son being interrogated five times by a person called Skrbic. On the sixth time, and I'm quoting now from the second full paragraph, starting: "My son was interrogated five times. On the sixth time, I went to Slavko and pleaded with him to save my son." I'm sorry. He identifies you back on page 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could quickly go to page 8 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just find out to whom this statement was given?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The statement was given to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor. If we could go to -- no, the first page has contact details. Page 8, please, the second to last paragraph

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He said that it was his turn for interrogation and the interrogator was a lieutenant in the military police. He was wearing a camouflage uniform with two stars indicating the rank of lieutenant. The interrogator was my sister's daughter's neighbour. The lieutenant's name was Slavko Puhalic. So if we can go then on to page 11. He said then I saw Slavko, I went to Slavko and pleaded with him to save my son. That they were going to kill my child. I saw Slavko later and he called me to him. He said that he had spoken to Skrbic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly read slowly, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He had spoken to Skrbic and that my son had a gold chain. This meant that we had to pay him with a gold chain. I told Slavko that others had already taken the chain but that I had 150 German marks. He took the money and later came to see me and said that he had talked to Skrbic and it would not happen again. Now, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I remember perhaps after coming here that the son's name was Ajdin, if I got it right. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I will confirm that after the lunch break, Your Honours. Is this a good time to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. We will have a break for 45 minutes and we will resume at 1.38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zenkic's son is, in fact, you said, Ajdin. It's A-j-d-i-n. It's on page 7 of his statement. So you do recall taking the money from Rifet Zenkic in order so that his son was not going to be further beaten by Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I remember that family.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalic, could you come closer to the microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you said that it was a family of neighbours of mine, now I recall that family. They insisted that I help that gentleman, Zenkic, I think you said the name was, and I went -- that was perhaps 800 metres, one kilometre, outside the camp. I found that family, and I told him to go to the camp, that that was the safest place, the safest option. He didn't accept that so I returned to the camp and I had no clue what was going on later, and I have no idea about this money you are talking about. I tried to help that person. He didn't accept. Now, what happened after that, I really couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There are three microphones on now at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Line 9, the witness said: No, then I remember family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You know the camp guard called Bosko Lakic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember. I did not have any communication with the guards. It was not my job. It was up to Mr. Kuruzovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You went to places in the camp where women were housed, including the wooden shack, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about. The women were around the camp, inside the camp, under tents, in trucks, in cars, wherever it was possible to sleep, to rest, women were everywhere, together with children and men. All those who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There was also a place, a wooden shack, where women were sleeping. You didn't attend there with a flash light and call women out at night-time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So this is what Slobodan Kuruzovic, the camp commander, said about the rape allegations when was interviewed: "Perhaps it's not nice to say it now because it's an ugly situation but the older Muslims that were in there were also making jokes on that because we are that kind of people. Had the older lady said that she had a nice time. It's not nice to say but that's what I heard, like two days after." And then he goes on to say: "Well, that's how it was, probably some sort of a prank. I don't think anyone was seriously physically injured."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do we have that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's at -- oh, it's, sorry, transcript page 14829 which is a couple of pages into the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: For the record, this is actually testimony in the Stakic case not an interview with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, yes, you're correct. Thank you, Mr. Robinson. It was the Stakic testimony given on the 31st of March, 2003. And what I read was from lines 12 to 16. And then lines 20 to 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And it's referring to when he was interviewed the year before, and Mr. Malik [phoen] asked him, What, you mean the person who was raped? She said how nice it was? And you answered, Yes, whether she was raped now but I don't know. Well, anyway, there were no test results of any real differation [phoen] or any real deperation [phoen] or anything because I just had other things to take care of in my mind. So Mr. Puhalic this captures in a nutshell, doesn't it, how the camp commander viewed allegations of rape or sexual assault in his camp, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: As regards that lady, who stated that, that was rape. I cannot exactly remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Puhalic, if I can just stop you there. The part that I read out to you in private session, I do not want you to repeat that person's name. We were in private session at that point. The -- the allegations that are being discussed now with Mr. Kuruzovic are the rape allegations in relation to a number of women complaining that they had been taken out of the camp and raped, so two different situations here. My point to you is, though, this captures, does it not, exactly the camp commander's views as to what he thought about allegations being made about rape and sexual assault in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No. I wish to explain precisely what Mr. Kuruzovic said to this person. That was the person that was raped, with five or six other women or even up to seven. When I came to Trnopolje in the morning, the commander was not there, and when I went into the camp, a lady walked up to me and said that her child had been raped and that really shook me, as a person, and I immediately asked where that girl was, and she said, That's my daughter. Among other things, the girl said that she was not there all by herself. There was another person there with her. And I asked her whether she knew who that person was, and she said, Well, I cannot remember now the name, but anyway I did find these six or seven women, and, among other things that Major Kuruzovic said, one of them said this by way of a joke, or maybe she meant it seriously, I don't know. She said that about that man, so I remember that part, I remember that, and when the commander, Kuruzovic, came, I reported that to him so that further activities could be undertaken. The doctor also came. I found these persons. I brought them down there. I mean some were outside the camp, now was it three or four women that were outside the camp, and I think the three were from the camp, I mean this young girl and these two women, so the doctor did --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The women were, in fact, taken to a hospital and examined. You said that -- that the persons responsible were arrested for these rapes. What are their names?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember now exactly what the name was of that young man. I took part in his arrest. And the police -- actually, these women told me where this was in Kozarac. I went there with the military police and civilian police; that is to say my own life was in jeopardy. I went among the soldiers in order to arrest that man or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can stop you there, these -- this person or these people were never prosecuted, were they, for these rapes that they committed in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: That I don't know. I'm telling you now that this person, that is to say that did take part, but he was not the one who actually raped the girl. This girl - there were two sisters there, actually - she said that this man that we arrested had some kind of a ring on his hand and that he actually helped stop them from raping her. We stayed at the command - now, I may be wrong - for two or three hours for the questioning but while I was at the command, these young men who did that, that group, called the command and they said, and I'm quoting now: That they would attack Prijedor if this young man is not released. I went from there -- I'm sorry, let me just finish. I returned to the camp. The next day this group came with two tanks to the camp and I heard this sound. I realised something was happening. I managed to have the soldiers removed from the road.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The civilians were supposed to be in the school and in other buildings. They came there. They disarmed me. I stayed on the road all by myself in front them. The commander was not there. I was there on my own. The commander was not there. And there was this Albanian there, Izet Beri, the one who was there. Since I realised that these men were rather drunk, I asked him for a bottle of brandy or some kind of alcohol. He gave it to me, I gave it to them, and I somehow managed to persuade them not to shoot. I don't know. I don't know how. That's how it all end.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the bottom line is [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the bottom line is they were never prosecuted for committing these rapes in Trnopolje camp; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: That I don't know. I'm telling you. I'm not the one who can be the judge of that, who did what, and whether certain activities were carried out. I could not check that. I was just an ordinary soldier. I've been telling you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And neither were any investigations conducted in relation to the killings that occurred in the camp or the beatings that occurred in the camp; that's right, isn't it? To your knowledge there was never any investigations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, no. Most --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned briefly in paragraph 11 that there was an infirmary at the camp which provided medical assistance, and you said that there were one or two doctors as well as two or three nurses. And you mentioned earlier in your testimony today that there was a doctor of Serb ethnicity as well. But you know full well that it was a make-shift clinic with inadequate medical supplies for the thousands of detainees that were in the Trnopolje camp, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, just for the transcript, before we get the answer. Line 16, the interpreters did not hear the witness say: Major Kuruzovic took care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also said in paragraph 21 of your statement, and this is in relation to adjudicated fact 1230, that Trnopolje was never fully surrounded by soldiers, that there were no machine-gun nests or fire points holding guns against the camp. That's completely untrue, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No, there --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalic, could you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, apart from the witnesses who have given evidence in this trial, which said that there were guard posts surrounding the camp. And, in particular, I take Your Honours and Mr. Karadzic to -- to P03880. There is also an independent witness who testified when he visited the camp in late August, early September, and he said this, "So it appeared to be the site of a former school," and I'm reading from P00712, the testimony of Charles McLeod. He said: "So it appeared to be the site of a former school, the camp was bounded on two sides by a road. At the apex of the two roads there was a machine-gun covering down the two roads, pointing inwards to cover down the two roads. The camp was called an open reception centre." Dr. Mrdjanic [phoen], who testified - and this is P03880 - that the guard posts were around Trnopolje. All around Trnopolje there were guard posts. And that's at transcript page 7732. He then says on transcript page 7753: There was a machine-gun nest on this check-point here, when he's pointing out on a map. So it's just completely untrue for you to say that there were no guard posts around the camp and no machine-gun nests, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember that, but maybe. I don't know. A soldier put his rifle down next to the place where he was standing guard. But when I was passing there, I mean, I did not see civilians held at gunpoint, no. While I was there, that is to say, I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 19, you say in relation to adjudicated fact 1225, that no one came to Trnopolje by force, and the evidence in this case shows that the overwhelming majority of people didn't come to Trnopolje of their own volition, they were, in fact, rounded up and brought to the camp on buses and on foot. You know that, and you knew that then, that this was the case, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. I was not present at any one of those times. Somebody being brought on a bus. I know that people came on tractors, trucks, cars. There were a lot of cars, and I cannot --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry to -- to -- to interrupt you there. They came on buses. They were -- it was organised. They were rounded up, and they were brought to the camp on buses. They were rounded up from Kozarac. They were rounded up from Jazkici [phoen]. They were rounded up from Trnopolje. They were rounded up from the Bodoje [phoen] in July after the cleansing at the end of July. Witnesses have testified here that they were rounded up and bought to the camp against their will. Now, you're saying that you didn't see any of these buses in the 24 or 25 or 26-odd days that you were at the camp.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, you just mentioned July, June, and I said that from the 10th or 11th June I wasn't there until the 18th of June; that is to say I was not present when this happened. As for what I saw, I'm telling you about that. I'm not sure. Maybe sometime in the beginning, when there was this attack on Prijedor, maybe -- I don't know. I'm telling you, I'm not sure. I cannot remember. Perhaps some were brought then. But then Kozarac -- people went on foot because there was fighting going on and people did not have time to put people onto buses because people were fleeing while the fighting was going on. They were trying to save their bare lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The evidence is that they were put on buses. They were taken on foot. They were escorted by soldiers. Now, according to your evidence, after the first few days, security of the camp was increased to protect the civilians, yes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, that's not correct. In fact, security was increased because of a fear of a breakout from the camp. That's the real reason, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember. Perhaps somebody did leave. Perhaps somebody did escape. I cannot say because I was not the one who was in charge of monitoring that. I told you, I was in charge of food and things like that. I've already said I cannot tell you about that. It would be best for you to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it would be best for me to what? The interpreter -- I -- I -- I came in too quickly and I apologise. You didn't finish your answer. The interpreter didn't catch the end of your answer. It would be best for me to do what?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: It was Commander Kuruzovic who knew best about all of that that was going on, Major Kuruzovic, whatever, about all of these things that were happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, you say that the Trnopolje camp was -- was this place where people could come and that nobody was detained, no guards. In fact, it's not that way at all. It was set up because in the beginning -- and the guards were increased because of this fear of a breakout.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can have 65 ter number 1D05886. Now, this is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is dated the 31st of May, and it's a Croatian intercept. And it says: This is -- there is a collection camp for the non-Serb population in Trnopolje village at the stadium. The enemy fears a breakout from the camp or an escape, so an order has been issued for security to be stepped up, and, if necessary, tripled. If it's a camp where everyone is free to come and go, as you say it is, then why are they tripling security for fear of people breaking out? Breaking out of where?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, again --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: They camp where they are being held --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I did not understand what it was that you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm saying that they are breaking out of the camp where they are being held by the Serb authorities. That was the view, that they didn't want them to break out. They were being held. You said in paragraph 7 of your statement that people could leave to go and get food, but they had to leave their ID documents. And you also repeated it in paragraph 9 in a slightly different way saying that they were allowed to freely leave the camp after reporting to the guard and leaving a document. So basically they weren't free to leave the area, were they? Because if the authorities at the camp had their identification papers, they couldn't go anywhere, could they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know now whether it was Commander Kuruzovic who said that to do that, but there were people who went without documents, went home to get, say, a blanket for the night or some food. There were some people who would go home and take a bath and come back because of their personal hygiene. Things like that did happen. As for this breakthrough, I have no idea. But maybe -- maybe -- I mean -- well, in a car, I actually found a pistol, 9 millimetres. A Muslim gentleman had that pistol, and perhaps there might have been some other weapons there, I cannot say, so that kind of thing did happen, too, within the camp. But usually -- I'm sorry, allow me to finish. Now, why were soldiers there? There was a war already in -- on in Bihac, Cazin, and we thought that there might be some revanchism because refugees were already coming in and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I am actually doing that right now, answering your question. If refugees are coming in from Bihac, of Serb ethnicity, the army wanted to prevent any kind of retaliation, so that -- well, after all, there were quite a few civilians who had uniforms, so people had to be protected, and it's from that point of view, people who went home in order to come back, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalic -- sorry, sorry, sorry. My question to you was people -- people are not free to leave if their identification papers have been left with the camp authorities. It's not a camp -- it's not a camp where you can walk in and out and go wherever you please. You were keeping the detainees' documents so they couldn't go anywhere but back to the camp when they were actually going out to get food.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that right now. I don't know why, but there is this probability, precisely for people to go back in order for the records to be kept. Where could a person go? How do I explain all of this to you? Actually, with all these documents, to show that he or she was a Muslim. Where could they go?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Bosnian Serb military and political authorities also saw Trnopolje camp as a detention facility? In -- in correspondence - and this is D01872 - they refer to it as -- when they are talking about closing the Trnopolje prisoner of war camp, they also refer to it in -- in another military document, P03721. When they are talking about a decision of the RS Presidency on granting amnesty for criminal prosecution it talks about prisoners of war in Manjaca and Trnopolje prisons. So it wasn't an open camp as you make it out to be, was it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 1D09763, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just -- actually, there will be too much left for re-examination. Perhaps this could be clarified with the witness, what the "no" referred to. It was a complex question with double negation in our language and that doesn't work in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer? This was a centre of an open type.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. If it was a centre of an open type, then --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can look at 1D09763 and it not be broadcast, please, and if we can go to page 42.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is the Prijedor hospital protocol book, log-book. And at the 17th of June, 1992, we see an entry there for Salih Softic [phoen], a prisoner from Trnopolje. So, again, it begs the question: Why call him a prisoner from Trnopolje if it's the open camp that you say it was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I don't see that here. Where is he being called a prisoner? I cannot see where that is written.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Second -- the second entry from the bottom, entry 3349. I'm sorry, on page 62. Do you see it there now?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So why -- why call him a prisoner from Trnopolje, if it's an open camp, then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. You have to ask the person who wrote that. I cannot say anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I tender that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we mark it for identification?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, until we get an English translation. And I'm just -- for privacy reasons perhaps we can redact the other names on that page except for the one that I've just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Give the number again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be MFI P6501.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Registrar. Your Honour, I would also ask for the intercept to be MFI'd, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI P6502, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said in paragraph 10 of your statement that you helped people get safe passage and also helped to get approval from Kuruzovic. Approval from what? For what -- approval from Kuruzovic for what?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, it was - how should I put it? - a kind of a pass for the people who were in the camp, that they could pass through a check-point held by the police or something like that, and take people to the town to a family where they would go further, be transported or something like that, where they would find their further residence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, what's the reason why you don't want to give the names of these people you helped to get safe passage?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: It's not a problem. I can, for example -- I don't know. I can't remember now and here all the first and last names, but this Izet Beri family from Kozarac, ethnic Albanians, and others also, other Albanians from Prijedor. I know they were called Piste or something like that. Then Mr. Idriz Hosic [phoen], who was a former football player who played for the Yugoslav team. Then there was a Rajkovic [phoen] family. They were Croats. And let me not list others that I can't remember now. But there were many others, let me not say, a hundred or perhaps more people whom I transported and helped them to find where they would leave via Croatia or whichever route they would take to go further, I wouldn't know that. But I do know that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... sorry.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: But I do know that to this day, some of these people who visit Prijedor come also to see me. They drop by and they want in a way to return the favour that I did them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We will get to you transporting them in a moment, but once the authorities had decided what was to be done with the detainees, convoys were organised on a regular basis, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I was present in one convoy in which I don't know how or what, but there were buses. People were boarded on the buses and transported in the direction of Travnik or Turbe. I wouldn't know exactly. I don't know. Major Kuruzovic was there and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When was -- when was that and how many were in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you exactly now whether it was perhaps around what date it was. I couldn't specify that. But, well, that was what I saw, that people left. Now, where, I think it was Travnik or thereabouts, but I cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, we will try and pinpoint it. Was it before or after your spa treatment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I can't -- I can't lie to you. I'm not sure. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, sorry, you came back from your spa treatment around the 17th of July. Was it shortly after you came back?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As Mr. Kuruzovic's logistics officer, as you say you were, what, if anything, did you have to do to co-ordinate these convoys?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't have anything to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you said that there were no preparations before the journalists came, talking about foreign media now, their visit in early -- 5th of August. And after they left, you said wire was neither put up or removed. But, of course, we have just established that you weren't there then. According to the calculations, I think you came back to the camp on the 17th of July and you said you spent between 10 and 15 days there. So that puts it up to the end of -- around the end of July or the 1st -- 1st of August, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, but there was a team of journalists. Now, when they came, once again, I can't tell you exactly when that was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was there? The videotape that you saw this morning had the English journalists with the pink shirt on, Penny Marshall. Were you there that day of that visit of those particular journalists on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I wasn't there then, but this journalist -- I'm not sure whether it was one team that was also perhaps from Geneva, perhaps from the Red Cross or something. I don't know. I think that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalic, you would remember this, I would assume. It's the first time any journalist got into the camp. So were you -- were you at the camp on the day the very first journalists got -- came to the camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: If this is the footage from the first time when someone visited, then I was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: All right. So you said that there was no wire that was put up before they came or after they left. And, in fact, we have evidence in the case to say that there was wire put up before they came and that it was -- that it was taken down after the first visit and before the second visit, before they came back again, ITN. Let me just show you two short clips.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could play, please, P03785. This is the video of the first visit. And play from 19.50 to 20.06, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you see that fence there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that was put up when the men from Keraterm were transferred there, weren't -- wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay, if we can have 65 ter 40168G, please. It's another short clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "There's now some food getting through, although the queues are long, and there's also shelter and clothes provided by the Serbian authorities. And the barbed wire fence which shocked the world has been torn down from its posts. All this has been done in advance of the simultaneous arrival of the Red Cross and our cameras. For certain conditions here have improved these refugees are safer. But the Red Cross have still not been allowed to enter any other camps and our visits are closely supervised."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now having reviewed the video footage, is it -- is your memory refreshed about the fence coming down?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, the reporter there said that the International Red Cross still weren't allowed into the camp. They didn't come into the camp until around the 10th of August, 1992, did they? And it was at that point that the -- that the detainees were properly formally registered.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I couldn't confirm that for you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you said that you left at the end of -- oh -- oh -- on --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, can I tender this clip, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection so long as the commentary is not included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, since he wasn't present, it falls into the same situation as the clip that we played. When we played the clip, the Prosecution asked that the commentary of the journalist not be included, and so this would be the same situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, in the Defence video-clip the commentary was included with the understanding that it was added by Serbian media.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, maybe I misunderstood, but I thought that you said that that would not be included. And you asked me if we were not tendering that part of it, and I -- or not offering that part of it, and I confirmed it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably I didn't make myself clear but -- yes, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I was actually on the same wave-length as Mr. Robinson. I thought that the commentary by the people that were interviewing was being admitted but not the commentary of the makers of the documentary. That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was only me, then. So you have no objection to admit without the sound?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6503, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, it was after this -- it was after this first visit by the foreign journalists that Kuruzovic put up a sign to say open reception centre, and it was written both in English and Serbo-Croatian on the Red Cross centre across the road from the camp; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay, so -- sorry. You don't know because by the beginning of August or certainly -- sorry. You say that you were in the camp on the 5th of August. So at what time -- at what point after did you go back to your unit? You mentioned to us earlier this morning that you came back to the camp on the 17th of July, spent 10 or 15 days there, and then went back to your unit. We have now established that you were, in fact, there until at least the 5th of August which is when this ITN crew arrived. So how long after this crew were there did you leave the camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you, I don't know whether that was the TV crew or whether it was another TV crew. I cannot claim that with any certainty. But what you're asking me now, I don't know when exactly I returned, but the audio recording and this wire, I did not see that, and I cannot say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I help? On page 50, line 9, witness said till what time he probably was there. I'll not tell the date, not to instruct witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. That's exactly my point. The witness said that he came back to the camp on the 17th of July, stayed 10 or 15 days, which to my calculation was around the 1st of August, and he said that he went back to his unit. In fact, he's just testified a moment ago that he was present when one media group came to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Puhalic, I put it to you that you would remember if it was the very first visit, and you said that you were there for the first visit which means that you were still in the camp on the 5th of August. So my question -- I'll repeat it: How long after this visit did you leave the camp? Were you there days, were you there weeks? Did you stay until the camp closed at the end of October -- in November?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No, no. I -- well, I'm telling you I don't know which TV crew was there. I know that it was a lady from Geneva. She was there then. And that she did conduct an interview inside, probably I'm also somewhere in the footage. She talked to the civilians and the staff and the others there inside. Now, whether I stayed there after that -- but it could have been perhaps until around -- as far as I remember, it was -- whether it was before August, I can't remember, or perhaps even in July. I can't remember exactly. Well, in this context, how long after that I stayed there in Trnopolje, two or three days after that, because I was told that I should return to the unit. I can't remember exactly how long it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think my time is nearly up. I was going to ask, given the additional three pages and ten paragraphs in the statement that we received -- I have dealt with a couple of the matters but there are two other areas that I would like to deal with the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much longer time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think I could do it in 10 or 15 minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But I'm not a good one for time, as Your Honour well knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalic, you said -- you said in paragraph 13 that many wanted to leave Prijedor municipality because of the war, to save their lives, and most probably -- and most of them probably did not want to take part in the war. You'd agree that given what had taken place with the property of the non-Serbs and their loved ones, that they were fearful for their lives, were they not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course they were in fear. We, who were in town, were also in fear, and fearful for our lives. I was fearful for the lives of my family and my children. Now that you say this [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, the vast majority of them [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] With regard to Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With regard to Mr. Who?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to mention this gentleman that you asked me about, a little while ago, about his son, Ajdin, that family --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalic, I've moved on from Mr. Zenkic and his -- his family. You have answered my question. You said that they were fearful for their lives, as were yourself.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You know that the vast majority of them had no home to return to because it had either been shelled or burnt and that the atmosphere was of such a coercive nature that people felt that they had no choice but they had to leave. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, they had nowhere to return, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Around the end of September, beginning of October, around 1500 left the Trnopolje camp on buses for Karlovac in Croatia. You're -- you're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you aware that there were still around 3.000 people left in Trnopolje in October and November?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 25609. This is a report of the Serb Red Cross dated the 30th of September, 1992, for the period 5 May to 30th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we switch to e-court again?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 9, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It says there that, middle of the page in the English, 23.000 people have been housed through the reception centre at Trnopolje, of whom we and the International Red Cross have dispatched 1.561 to the Karlovac reception centre. On the 29th of September, 1992, a convoy was escorted to Karlovac in the presence of European observers. The problem of Trnopolje is becoming more complicated with the onset of autumn so that all those who have been left without homes and arriving in great numbers seeking accommodation -- so that all those who have been left without homes are arriving in great numbers seeking accomodation. There are now more than 3.000 citizens there. And then it goes on a couple of -- a paragraph down. There is great pressure for citizens of Muslim or Croatian nationality to leave the autonomous region of Krajina. That sets out how it was at the time, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I agree with you to a point, and to a certain extent I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What do you agree with me about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I agree with this part where it says that there were families who had nowhere to return and who asked to go further on for their own safety. And what I do not agree with, it's that the Muslim population, which used to live in town and left their homes, they went further on. There was no work and people did leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Would you agree that that figure of 23.000 who have been housed through the reception centre is -- is -- is about right? That's what -- that's what you recall?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, even in relation to -- to the logistics for the food, you were aware of how many people were in the camp, were you not? So how many -- how many people were in the camp at any one time, roughly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, what do I know? Perhaps around -- when I was there, perhaps around 2.000 to 3.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And do you agree, because for the reasons that we've discussed a moment ago, that there was pressure put on the citizens of Muslims and Croat nationalities to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, perhaps not such pressure but those who had nowhere to survive, the winter was coming, they needed to live on, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: It's not for the redirect. It's an interpretation of the pressure put on the citizens. So I would like this to be clarified. Who was pressing?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it not discussed in previous questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6504, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The Trnopolje camp was inspected by CSCE mission in late August/early September 1992. A rapporteur called Sir John Thompson from the United Kingdom was leading this mission, and I just want to read to you what he concluded after inspecting the camp. And this was -- the inspection took place sometime between the 29th of August and the 4th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 05616C, please. And if we could go to page 25 of the report, I think this 65 ter number has the first page and then pages 25 and 26.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's not been released, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We do have 05616 without any letters after it. That's [indiscernible] page document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, this is just an excerpt from that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we see just 5616?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that and go to page 25 of that. Are we going to page 25?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is page 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can -- 25 on the bottom of the -- bottom of the page, if we can go -- can we see the next page over to see what it is? Yeah, that memorandum on Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we can see there in the second paragraph, the second sentence, this is what's concluded after inspecting Trnopolje: These people are living in terror and the CSCE mission believe they have substantial reasons for their fears. And down to the last sentence in that paragraph: Whatever their long-term hopes, no one wishes in present circumstances to return to their homes in Western Bosnia because the local administration cannot and will not guarantee their physical security. Now, this is -- this is the situation as it was at that time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I don't know what this is about. I don't understand. Who is going back to Western Bosnia? What is this all about?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a report by the CSCE mission. And you can see on -- in the second paragraph the number of inmates at the centre of whom great majority, if not all, are of the Muslim faith is currently thought to be in the neighbourhood of 2.000. And then it goes on to say these people are living in terror and they believe that they have substantial reasons for their fears. And I'm saying that this document is consistent with what you testified to earlier, when you agreed with me that the non-Serb population were in fear of their life and that they had no choice but to go because of the atmosphere that was -- was being created at the time. And that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, believe me, if I had a choice, I would have gone somewhere safer to stay alive, and I suppose that's what they did too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. I'm sorry, may I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. It deals with the period of 29 August, and on which is the time he said he wasn't there, so any -- and he also hasn't been able to confirm any of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I asked him whether this was consistent with --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At the time, when you were -- I'll be clearer. Mr. Puhalic, when were you in Trnopolje camp -- we discussed it a moment ago, and you agreed with me that the non-Serb population were in fear, that there was a coercive atmosphere, that they -- they didn't -- they couldn't stay. They had nowhere to stay. They had no home to go to. And I said to you this document is consistent with what we have just discussed, isn't it? And I must say your answer was -- was not responsive to my question. You said if you had a choice you would have gone somewhere safer to stay alive. But you said -- no, you did. You said, I suppose that's what they did too. And that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: In this context I would have gone myself, if I had had somewhere to go because we, too, were in fear of the war simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit the cover page and this page, page 25.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6505, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue tomorrow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I agree, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalic, we will continue tomorrow morning but I'd like to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. President, the Chamber ordered us to upload a revised translation for Exhibit P6455 by today's date and that has been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 14th day of November, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.58 p.m.,
